paragraphs: TabPFN v2 makes predictions on tabular datasets through in-context learning, despite substantial differences in what their columns represent. This paper investigates how it handles that heterogeneity and whether its existing capabilities can be extended to datasets with many features, many categories, or large numbers of examples.

The authors find that TabPFN v2 can recover relationships between attributes even when their input tokens are randomized. This indicates that learning separate attribute embeddings for each dataset is unnecessary for handling heterogeneity in the studied setting. They also turn the model into a feature extractor and find that its representations separate prediction targets well, helping explain its predictive accuracy.

To broaden its use, the paper introduces a divide-and-conquer strategy applied at test time. This addresses the stated dimensionality, category-count, and scale limitations without retraining the model. Together, the findings connect its predictive success to relationships and representations it already learns, while showing that inference design can extend the usefulness of a pretrained tabular model.
neurips-2025-a-closer-look-at-tabpfn-v2-.tldr: TabPFN v2 learns useful attribute relationships and separable features, while a test-time divide-and-conquer strategy extends its capabilities without retraining.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decisions where losses can be adversarial but the available action sets arise stochastically. Its goal is to keep regret—the accumulated loss relative to the best policy—small while remaining computationally practical, including when each round offers a very large number of possible actions.

The algorithm converts this contextual problem into an adversarial linear bandit problem with fixed actions that tolerates model misspecification. Without knowing the context distribution or using a context simulator, it achieves regret bounded by the smaller of d²√T and √(d³T log K), up to logarithmic factors. Its running time is polynomial in feature dimension, round count, and the number of constraints describing available actions.

This resolves the stated open question about obtaining polynomial-in-dimension, square-root-in-time regret without runtime dependence on the action count. The result also covers combinatorial action sets described by polynomially many linear constraints. When a simulator is available, the regret guarantee improves to a bound depending on the square root of the best policy’s cumulative loss.
neurips-2025-an-improved-algorithm-for-a.tldr: A reduction yields an efficient contextual bandit algorithm with square-root-in-time regret even when the number of available actions is large.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate decisions for reinforcement learning, with an energy function guiding generation toward desirable behavior. The difficulty is determining the appropriate guidance at intermediate generation steps. The required quantity involves the logarithm of an expectation, making it intractable to evaluate directly in the formulation studied here.

Analytic Energy-guided Policy Optimization, or AEPO, develops an analytical route to estimating that quantity. The authors first derive a closed-form expression for intermediate guidance when the diffusion model satisfies a conditional Gaussian transformation. They then examine the posterior Gaussian distribution within the expression and obtain an estimation target under assumptions described as mild.

An intermediate energy neural network is trained to approximate that target, connecting the analysis to a usable policy optimization method. Evaluations cover more than 30 offline reinforcement learning tasks, with reported improvements over numerous representative baselines on D4RL. The contribution is an analytically motivated way to train diffusion guidance; its closed-form result specifically depends on the stated Gaussian condition.
neurips-2025-analytic-energy-guided-poli.tldr: AEPO uses Gaussian-based analysis to train intermediate energy guidance for diffusion policies, outperforming numerous baselines on offline reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Selecting diverse language-model training data requires deciding which examples are similar. Common practice uses embeddings from models trained for tasks such as retrieval, but similarity useful for retrieval may not reflect similarity useful for pretraining. This paper develops a framework for evaluating that fit directly.

The framework examines three aspects of an embedding model. First, it tests whether distances between examples reflect how pretraining loss generalizes between them. Second, it uses the embeddings in a standard diversity-based selection procedure, then trains a language model on the selected data and measures downstream performance. Third, it checks whether embeddings distinguish examples originating from different data sources.

Experiments use the Pile and pretrain a 1.7-billion-parameter language model on 200 billion tokens. In this setting, standard off-the-shelf embeddings perform worse for data curation than even simple embeddings extracted from models trained on the same corpus. The findings motivate assessing similarity through its consequences for pretraining, and provide concrete criteria for designing embeddings suited to that purpose.
neurips-2025-analyzing-similarity-metric.tldr: A pretraining-focused evaluation finds that common embedding models select data less effectively than simple embeddings from models trained on the same corpus.

paragraphs: Fog, snow, and darkness degrade the visual evidence needed to understand a scene. CroPe addresses this problem by supplementing visual features with textual semantic information. The aim is to help a model form more consistent representations across adverse conditions when appearance alone becomes less reliable.

Its text-generation module creates complementary text embeddings at multiple levels. These embeddings combine information intended to generalize across conditions with information sensitive to the particular domain. A second module then integrates this textual information into the visual representation using unified attention and a reverse decoding chain. Fusion proceeds from deeper features rich in semantic information toward shallower features with less semantic content.

This ordering makes semantic compensation part of the feature-processing pipeline, allowing textual information to support multiple levels of visual understanding. The authors report competitive results across the adverse conditions evaluated, with improvements over prior state-of-the-art performance of 6.5 mIoU on ACDC-Night and 1.2 mIoU on ACDC-All. These results support the usefulness of combining visual and textual representations for the studied adverse-scene tasks.
neurips-2025-crope-cross-modal-semantic-.tldr: CroPe supplements degraded visual features with multi-level textual information, improving scene understanding on adverse-condition benchmarks.

paragraphs: People’s preferences can change with the alternatives presented alongside a choice. These context effects may involve pairs of options or more complicated interactions among several options. DeepHalo models this behavior while addressing a difficulty in existing feature-based approaches: restrictive interaction structures or mixtures of interaction orders that are hard to interpret.

The proposed neural framework uses features describing alternatives and lets the modeler explicitly control interaction order. This makes it possible to identify effects systematically according to whether they arise from pairwise or higher-order relationships. The approach therefore connects prediction with an organized account of how the composition of a choice set influences decisions.

The paper also establishes a universal approximation result when DeepHalo is specialized to the featureless setting. That expressiveness claim is specific to that setting. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show strong predictive performance alongside greater transparency into the factors driving choices. Together, these results suggest a way to study contextual preferences without losing the ability to distinguish different orders of interaction.
neurips-2025-deephalo-a-neural-choice-mo.tldr: DeepHalo models how available alternatives influence choices while allowing explicit control and interpretation of interaction order.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models can scale efficiently in computation while still demanding substantial memory for their parameters. Shapley-MoE aims to reduce that burden by identifying which experts contribute most and pruning others. It bases importance on Shapley values from cooperative game theory, which assess contributions in the context of different expert combinations.

Exact computation is impractical, so the method approximates these values through Monte Carlo sampling with quadratic complexity. Two refinements improve that approximation. Early Truncation stops unstable sampling steps associated with excessively small expert subsets. Router-Guided Importance Sampling uses gating activation probabilities to prioritize important subsets. Theoretical and experimental analyses support improvements in both estimation accuracy and efficiency.

The resulting pruned models outperform existing expert-pruning methods in the reported evaluations. For Qwen2-57B-A14B, removing 25% of experts increases perplexity by 0.92 while preserving over 96.4% of average zero-shot accuracy. This example shows how a contribution-based pruning criterion can remove substantial expert capacity while retaining much of the measured predictive performance.
neurips-2025-discovering-important-exper.tldr: Shapley-MoE efficiently estimates expert contributions to prune mixture-of-experts models while retaining much of their measured performance.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning extracts representations without labels, but much of its development assumes clean data. This paper targets representation learning under substantial noise, aiming to make the learned model robust enough that deployment requires neither a separate denoiser nor downstream fine-tuning.

The method does use a denoiser during pretraining. It first learns that denoiser from noisy data through self-supervision, then uses its outputs to create a curriculum that starts with denoised examples and progresses toward noisy ones. Teacher-guided regularization additionally encourages embeddings of noisy inputs to remain anchored to embeddings of their denoised counterparts. These two mechanisms encourage the backbone to absorb noise robustness into its representations.

After pretraining, the denoiser can be discarded, simplifying inference. On ImageNet-1k with a ViT-B backbone under extreme Gaussian noise, specified as sigma 255 and an SNR of 0.72 dB, the method reports a 4.8% improvement in linear probing accuracy over DINOv2. The result demonstrates denoiser-free inference robustness emerging from noise-aware pretraining in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2025-ditch-the-denoiser-emergenc.tldr: A denoised-to-noisy training curriculum helps self-supervised models internalize noise robustness so the denoiser can be discarded after pretraining.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems must rank discrete items despite observing only sparse evidence of user preferences. Diffusion-based recommenders address sparsity through a process of perturbing and reconstructing preferences, but many use continuous Gaussian noise. PreferGrow instead builds the process around discrete items and their relative preference ratios.

A positive ratio indicates that one item is preferred over another, directly connecting the representation to ranking. During the forward process, the method weakens preferences by replacing a preferred item with alternatives, in a procedure analogous to negative sampling. This preference fading avoids assuming a prior noise distribution. Reconstruction then iteratively strengthens the preference signal using estimated ratios.

The paper supplies a matrix-based formulation and theoretical analysis showing that PreferGrow retains key properties of discrete diffusion processes. Across five benchmark datasets, it outperforms existing diffusion-based recommenders in the reported experiments. Its main contribution is to align both the representation and the perturbation process with the discrete, comparative nature of recommendation, while using diffusion to learn from sparse preference observations.
neurips-2025-fading-to-grow-growing-pref.tldr: PreferGrow uses discrete preference fading and reconstruction to improve recommendation from sparse user data.

paragraphs: Two independently trained networks can look far apart in parameter space even when their learned functions are closely related. Parameter symmetries contribute to this mismatch: changing a network’s internal representation can preserve its function. This paper investigates how accounting for richer symmetries reveals straight interpolation paths with little or no loss barrier.

Earlier alignment methods largely focused on reordering neurons. The proposed framework includes permutations, semi-permutations, orthogonal transformations, and general invertible maps, bringing several previous approaches into a broader account of valid reparameterizations. This expanded set of transformations provides more ways to align independently trained Transformers before interpolating between their parameters.

Using the framework, the authors find low- and zero-barrier linear paths between independently trained Vision Transformers and GPT-2 models. They also extend alignment beyond pairs to multiple models and models of different widths. These findings show that some apparent separation between trained solutions can reflect parameterization choices, and that symmetry-aware alignment exposes connections missed by neuron reordering alone.
neurips-2025-generalized-linear-mode-con.tldr: A broader symmetry framework reveals low- and zero-loss-barrier linear connections between independently trained Transformers.

paragraphs: Benchmark prediction estimates a language model’s full evaluation score from a small subset of questions. The paper compares 11 methods across 19 benchmarks to investigate when this cost-saving strategy works. A strong baseline simply samples questions randomly and uses regression to predict unobserved results, outperforming most existing methods.

The central finding is that success depends heavily on similarity between models. Predicting scores among models resembling those already observed works better than predicting results for newly stronger models. In that extrapolation setting, none of the previous methods consistently improves on the average score from a random sample. This challenges both sophisticated subset selection and reliance on patterns learned from earlier models.

The authors introduce a method inspired by augmented inverse propensity weighting that consistently beats the random-sample average even during extrapolation. Its gains are generally modest, however, and it still depends on model similarity. The study therefore identifies a practical weakness at the evaluation frontier, where unfamiliar capabilities make reliable score prediction especially valuable.
neurips-2025-how-benchmark-prediction-fr.tldr: Predicting benchmark scores from small subsets becomes unreliable for newly stronger models, and a proposed improvement offers only modest gains.

paragraphs: Zero-shot policy transfer asks whether an agent trained in a fixed collection of environments can perform well in similar environments it has never encountered. Earlier work found that distilling a trained policy can sometimes improve this transfer. This paper investigates why that happens and what data should support the distillation process.

The authors prove a generalization bound under specified assumptions. The analysis points to two practical choices: train an ensemble of distilled policies and use as much data from the training environments as possible. These recommendations link the structure of the distilled predictor and the breadth of its training data to potential improvements on unseen environments.

Experiments then test these insights in broader settings where the theoretical assumptions no longer hold. The reported results support both recommendations, and an ensemble distilled on diverse data generalizes significantly better than the original agent. The paper thus combines a conditional theoretical explanation with empirical evidence that the resulting training guidance remains useful beyond the theory’s setting.
neurips-2025-how-ensembles-of-distilled-.tldr: Theory and experiments support using ensembles of policies distilled on broad training-environment data to improve transfer to unseen environments.

paragraphs: Complex knowledge questions often require several searches, with each result informing what to look for next. Irrelevant retrieved material can disrupt this process. ExSearch trains a language model to coordinate reasoning and retrieval, selecting useful information as its reasoning develops rather than treating retrieval as a single preliminary step.

Each step contains three actions: deciding what information is needed, calling an external retriever, and recording fine-grained evidence for subsequent reasoning. Training uses a Generalized Expectation-Maximization procedure. The model generates multiple search trajectories and assigns them importance weights, then updates itself using a loss reweighted by those values. Repeating these stages lets it learn from its own generated search behavior.

The authors provide a convergence analysis of this training process. Across four knowledge-intensive benchmarks, ExSearchS substantially outperforms the evaluated baselines, including a reported 7.8% improvement in exact match score. They also introduce ExSearch-Zoo to extend the approach to broader scenarios. The results support learning search as an iterative evidence-gathering capability integrated with reasoning.
neurips-2025-iterative-self-incentivizat.tldr: ExSearch improves agentic retrieval by repeatedly training a language model on importance-weighted search trajectories it generates itself.

paragraphs: Plug-and-play image restoration inserts a learned denoiser into an iterative reconstruction method. Standard convergence arguments often require properties of both the data-fitting term and denoiser that fail in Poisson imaging problems. Requiring a denoiser to be non-expansive can also restrict its denoising performance.

The paper proposes a cocoercive conservative denoiser, called CoCo, that may be expansive while supporting a convergence analysis. Its training strategy draws on generalized Helmholtz decomposition. Hamiltonian regularization promotes conservativeness, while spectral regularization ensures cocoerciveness. These conditions provide a different route to controlling the denoiser’s behavior without imposing the usual non-expansiveness requirement.

The authors prove that CoCo corresponds to a proximal operator of a weakly convex function, giving the restoration procedure an implicit weakly convex prior. They establish global convergence of the plug-and-play methods to a stationary point of that restoration model; this is not a claim of reaching a global optimum. Experiments report improvements over closely related methods in both visual quality and quantitative measures.
neurips-2025-learning-cocoercive-conserv.tldr: CoCo denoisers improve Poisson image restoration while enabling convergence to a stationary point under a weakly convex restoration model.

paragraphs: Neurosymbolic predictors combine neural perception with symbolic reasoning. A common simplification assumes that extracted symbols are conditionally independent, even when they interact. The paper argues that this limits the representation of uncertainty and dependencies, contributing to overconfident predictions and poor generalization outside the training distribution.

Neurosymbolic diffusion models address the issue by modeling symbols through a discrete diffusion process. Each individual step retains the independence assumption used by conventional predictors, keeping learning scalable. Across the sequence of steps, however, the model captures dependencies between symbols. This separates the computational convenience of a local assumption from the richer relationships represented by the overall process.

Experiments span synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including high-dimensional visual path planning and rule-based autonomous driving. The models achieve state-of-the-art accuracy among the neurosymbolic predictors evaluated and show strong calibration, meaning their confidence better reflects predictive reliability. The contribution is a way to combine scalable symbol prediction with joint dependency modeling and uncertainty quantification within the same neurosymbolic framework.
neurips-2025-neurosymbolic-diffusion-mod.tldr: Neurosymbolic diffusion models capture symbol dependencies across discrete diffusion steps, improving accuracy and confidence calibration.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting represents scenes with many explicit Gaussian primitives, enabling fast rendering but consuming substantial storage and memory. Reducing the primitive count can also reduce computation. However, a small set becomes more sensitive to errors from compressing its attributes, making compactness and rendering quality difficult to preserve together.

Optimized Minimal Gaussians, or OMG, addresses both the number of primitives and their attribute representation. It identifies distinct Gaussians among nearby ones to reduce redundancy without sacrificing quality. It then uses a compact, precise representation designed to capture both continuity and irregularity across primitives. A sub-vector quantization technique further represents irregularity with a negligible codebook size while maintaining fast training.

The experiments report nearly 50% lower storage requirements than the previous state of the art, together with rendering above 600 frames per second and high visual quality. These findings support jointly optimizing primitive count and attribute precision: reducing storage alone does not address the computational costs associated with retaining a large number of Gaussians.
neurips-2025-optimized-minimal-3d-gaussi.tldr: OMG combines fewer Gaussian primitives with precise compact attributes, reporting nearly 50% less storage and rendering above 600 FPS.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student to reproduce useful behavior from a larger teacher. Common logit-based methods add a separate distillation loss to cross-entropy, introducing a weight that requires careful tuning. PLD reframes the task as learning a ranking of classes using a choice-theoretic model.

Under the Plackett–Luce formulation, teacher logits act as scores expressing the worth of each class. PLD uses a confidence-weighted list-wise ranking loss to transfer information about the full class ordering. Its target places the true label first, then orders all remaining classes by the teacher’s confidence. This combines the correct answer with the teacher’s comparative judgments about other possibilities.

The resulting surrogate is convex, unchanged by a common shift in scores, and includes weighted cross-entropy as a special case. Experiments on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and MS-COCO show consistent gains across varied architectures and distillation objectives. Results include teacher–student pairs with matching and different architecture types, supporting the usefulness of class-ranking information across the evaluated distillation settings.
neurips-2025-pld-a-choice-theoretic-list.tldr: PLD distills a teacher’s confidence-weighted class ranking through a choice-theoretic loss, producing consistent gains across varied distillation settings.

paragraphs: Average treatment effect estimation concerns the difference in expected outcomes under treatment and control. This paper studies a setting where some units are known to have received treatment, while the treatment status of the remaining observed units is unknown. The unlabeled group therefore cannot simply be treated as an identified control group.

The authors connect this problem to positive-and-unlabeled learning and to causal estimation with missing data. They derive semiparametric efficiency bounds for the setting. These bounds describe the lowest asymptotic variance achievable by regular estimators, providing a statistical benchmark for how precisely treatment effects can be estimated as the sample grows.

The paper then constructs estimators that attain those bounds. The result establishes efficiency in the specified asymptotic sense, linking an achievable estimation procedure to the derived precision limit. Its contribution is therefore both a characterization of statistical uncertainty and a method that reaches that benchmark for the studied treated-and-unlabeled data setting, connecting causal inference with weakly supervised learning.
neurips-2025-puate-efficient-ate-estimat.tldr: PUATE derives statistical efficiency bounds and estimators that attain them when treatment status is known only for a treated subset.

paragraphs: Evaluating web agents requires testing both their ability to find information and their ability to complete actions across multiple steps. REAL provides controlled replicas of 11 widely used websites, covering activities such as shopping, travel, communication, and professional networking. Its benchmark contains 112 practical tasks modeled on complex everyday interactions.

Deterministic simulations make evaluations reproducible while keeping actions inside a controlled environment. The evaluation framework checks changes to website state programmatically for action tasks and uses rubric-guided language-model judgments for information retrieval. A flexible browser-based harness accepts black-box agent commands, supporting open-source and proprietary systems without requiring researchers to modify them.

In the reported experiments, the best success rate among frontier language models is 41%, indicating substantial difficulty with the benchmark’s navigation and completion requirements. The framework also supports adding tasks and generating post-training data at scale. REAL’s contribution combines realistic multi-step interactions with repeatable evaluation, making it possible to examine agent capability and reliability under consistent conditions.
neurips-2025-real-benchmarking-autonomou.tldr: REAL evaluates web agents on reproducible website simulations, where tested frontier models achieve at most 41% task success.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly aligns language models by maximizing average reward. That objective does not directly express how often the model produces low-reward outputs. Existing approaches that explicitly suppress undesirable outputs can reduce average-case performance, creating a tradeoff between typical quality and the probability of unwanted behavior.

RePULSe adds a targeted loss to the standard reinforcement learning objective. Learned proposals guide the sampling process toward low-reward outputs, and the added loss reduces their probability. This gives training a mechanism for locating and discouraging undesirable responses while retaining the usual objective that promotes high expected reward. Undesirability here is tied to the reward function used for alignment.

The experiments show a better tradeoff between expected reward and the probability of undesirable outputs than standard reinforcement learning alignment methods and the alternatives evaluated. They also report greater adversarial robustness. The findings support targeted sampling as a way to improve this balance, rather than establishing that unwanted outputs disappear entirely or that average performance must be sacrificed to reduce them.
neurips-2025-reducing-the-probability-of.tldr: RePULSe targets sampled low-reward responses during training, improving the tradeoff between average reward and undesirable-output probability.

paragraphs: Graph learning tasks can depend on interactions between distant nodes, which ordinary local message passing struggles to capture. This paper revisits ChebNet, an early spectral graph neural network, as a way to model those relationships. The authors find that its existing form is already competitive with classical message-passing networks and Graph Transformers on long-range benchmarks.

ChebNet’s polynomial construction also scales well at high orders, but the authors identify a related instability during training. They address it by recasting the network as a stable, non-dissipative dynamical system called Stable-ChebNet. The design supports stable information propagation with controllable dynamics, targeting the weakness uncovered in the original formulation.

Stable-ChebNet does not require eigendecompositions, positional encodings, or graph rewiring, and achieves near state-of-the-art results across several benchmarks. The findings show that revisiting an established spectral architecture can provide a competitive route to long-range graph learning. The improvement centers on stabilizing its propagation dynamics while retaining the useful scaling behavior of its polynomial approach.
neurips-2025-return-of-chebnet-understan.tldr: Stable-ChebNet stabilizes an early spectral graph network’s dynamics, achieving near state-of-the-art performance on long-range graph tasks.

paragraphs: Struct2D investigates whether multimodal language models can reason about three-dimensional environments through structured two-dimensional inputs. Its prompts combine bird’s-eye-view images, object marks, and object-centered metadata, with egocentric keyframes added when needed. The representation organizes perceptual evidence into a form that the language model can use for spatial reasoning.

Zero-shot analysis of closed-source models, including GPT-o3, finds strong performance on tasks such as relative direction estimation and route planning. Building on this result, the authors create Struct2D-Set through an automated pipeline that produces detailed question–answer pairs grounded in indoor 3D scenes. They use this dataset to fine-tune the open-source Qwen2.5VL model.

The tuned model relies on noisy 3D perception rather than ground-truth annotations, yet performs strongly across benchmarks involving 3D question answering, captioning, and object grounding, spanning eight reasoning categories. The findings support structured 2D representations as an effective interface between perception and language reasoning, without requiring explicit 3D representations as inputs to the multimodal language model.
neurips-2025-struct2d-a-perception-guide.tldr: Struct2D uses organized 2D views and object metadata to support strong 3D spatial reasoning in multimodal language models.

paragraphs: TimePerceiver treats time-series prediction as a coordinated problem of input encoding, output decoding, and training. It broadens the task beyond predicting future values to include interpolation and filling missing observations. Supporting these objectives requires a model that can handle observed and target segments located at arbitrary positions along the time axis.

The encoder uses latent bottleneck representations that interact with all input segments. These representations jointly capture relationships across time and across channels. The decoder uses learnable queries associated with target timestamps to retrieve relevant information for each requested prediction. This design explicitly connects where information is observed with where an output is needed.

The architecture is paired with a training strategy aligned to this generalized prediction setting. Across a wide range of benchmark datasets, the authors report consistent and significant improvements over prior state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a unified framework in which encoding, timestamp-aware decoding, and training jointly support multiple temporal prediction objectives, rather than treating forecasting solely as an encoder-design problem.
neurips-2025-timeperceiver-an-encoder-de.tldr: TimePerceiver unifies encoding, timestamp-based decoding, and training for extrapolation, interpolation, and imputation, with strong benchmark results.

paragraphs: Diffusion models may generate content that users want excluded, including inappropriate images, copyrighted material, or data associated with people requesting removal. This paper introduces a sampling-time method that uses a negation set of such examples to steer generation away from specified regions of the data distribution.

The approach directly modifies the sampling trajectory without retraining or fine-tuning the model. The authors derive a relationship between expected denoised samples associated with safe and unsafe regions, then use that relationship to construct a safe denoiser. Its stated guarantee concerns keeping final samples away from the area designated for negation, making the chosen exclusion region central to the method.

On large-scale datasets including CoPro, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art safety performance and substantially more cost-effective sampling than existing approaches. The contribution is therefore both a formal denoiser construction and a practical way to apply exclusions during generation. It makes the supplied negation set an actionable part of the sampling process while leaving the underlying model’s training untouched.
neurips-2025-training-free-safe-denoiser.tldr: A training-free denoiser uses a negation set to steer diffusion sampling away from specified unwanted regions.

paragraphs: Generated code can satisfy a requested function while still containing security or maintainability defects. This paper targets that gap with REAL, a reinforcement learning framework that uses automated program analysis as training feedback. The aim is to improve functional correctness and code quality together without relying on labor-intensive manual annotations.

REAL combines two supervision signals. Static analyzers detect issues such as security vulnerabilities and maintainability defects, while unit tests check whether the code behaves correctly. Both feed into reinforcement learning, allowing the model’s generated programs to be assessed through automated tools. The framework is described as prompt-agnostic and reference-free, so its supervision does not require a manually supplied reference solution.

Experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show improvements over state-of-the-art methods when functionality and quality are assessed simultaneously. These findings support including program-analysis feedback directly in model training. The contribution is a scalable way to make security and maintainability part of the learning objective alongside the functional behavior measured by tests.
neurips-2025-training-language-models-to.tldr: REAL trains code-generating models with static-analysis and unit-test feedback to improve functionality, security, and maintainability together.
